profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a global health NGO between the clinical lead for a new inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) care pilot and the regional health-systems operations manager. Three months after launch in two secondary hospitals in southern India, the pilot's monthly dashboard shows a sharp rise in 'treatment failures' and several pediatric patients flagged as overdue for cancer surveillance. Donors are asking whether the problem is poor adherence, inappropriate patient selection, supply interruptions, or a flaw in the care pathway itself. The meeting agenda is to diagnose why the pilot appears to be underperforming, identify the most likely root causes, and agree on an immediate corrective action that can be implemented before the next donor review. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan covering what to audit this week, what temporary fix to apply, and what evidence will count as the issue being resolved.

members.name: Dr. Asha Menon
members.expertise: Pediatric and adult gastroenterology, IBD management pathways, dysplasia and colorectal cancer surveillance in chronic colitis
members.background: A gastroenterologist trained in the UK who returned to India to help adapt IBD care models for lower-resource settings; she designed the pilot's clinical protocol and mentors local physicians at both hospitals.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the credibility of the clinical protocol and suspects the dashboard is exaggerating failure because field teams are operationalizing follow-up too narrowly; she is also worried that pediatric high-risk patients are quietly being missed if the surveillance schedule is being interpreted incorrectly.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a patient is 'stable,' it means steroid-free clinical remission maintained over at least two visits, not just temporary symptom improvement after induction.

The 'surveillance list' for IBD-related colorectal cancer naturally includes pediatric-onset colitis patients once disease duration crosses the protocol threshold, even if they are still being seen in pediatric clinics.
A 'stock-out issue' in this pilot usually means biologics were unavailable at the district hub pharmacy, because that is the bottleneck she has seen in prior programs.
A quick 'chart review' to troubleshoot pathway problems should include physician notes, pathology reports, and infusion logs rather than only the monthly dashboard export.

members.name: Ravi Kulkarni
members.expertise: Program operations, referral logistics, medicine procurement, indicator reporting, and scale-up in public-private hospital networks
members.background: An operations specialist who has run diabetes and oncology access programs across South Asia; he was brought in to make the IBD pilot financially scalable and donor-reportable across sites with uneven infrastructure.
members.private_state: He wants a fix that can be implemented cheaply and quickly before donor scrutiny intensifies; he suspects the apparent failures are mainly due to scheduling leakage and reporting artifacts, not a deeper flaw in treatment selection.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a patient is 'stable,' it means symptoms are controlled enough that the patient does not need escalation or unscheduled review that month.

The 'surveillance list' refers to the adult gastroenterology registry used for colonoscopy slot planning, because pediatric services are tracked separately and have not yet been integrated into the operations dashboard.

A 'stock-out issue' usually means the infusion chairs and day-care slots were unavailable locally even if the drug itself existed somewhere in the system, because service capacity is the practical limiting factor.
A quick 'chart review' for troubleshooting means reconciling the dashboard, pharmacy dispatch sheet, and appointment register, since those are the sources used for donor reporting.
If they agree to 'close the gap this month,' it means reducing overdue operational flags by the next reporting cycle rather than confirming durable clinical improvement.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a stable patient
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether patients were moved to maintenance only after they were 'stable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means steroid-free remission sustained across at least two visits with no active inflammatory warning signs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the patient looked controlled enough operationally to continue routine follow-up without urgent escalation that month.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In clinical programs, 'stable' is a routine shorthand everyone uses, so both hear a familiar, reasonable term and assume the other is using the obvious common meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: Which surveillance list is missing patients
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the surveillance list' when discussing overdue colorectal cancer surveillance.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the protocol-defined high-risk IBD surveillance cohort across pediatric and adult services.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the adult endoscopy scheduling list extracted from the operations registry.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is in fact a real list in each person's workflow, and both are used for surveillance-related decisions, so the phrase sounds perfectly specific without either realizing they are indexing different artifacts.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of fixing the pathway gap
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'close the gap' before the donor review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the gap is closed when chart-level review shows appropriate risk stratification and clinically correct follow-up plans for the affected patients.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the gap is closed when overdue flags and apparent treatment-failure counts drop on the next monthly dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They share the same urgent framing and both expect improvement quickly, so neither pauses to define the success condition behind the action phrase.

misalignment_points.topic: How the rapid audit will be done
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to do a 'chart review' this week to find the root cause.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes clinicians will manually inspect full medical records, including colonoscopy recommendations, pathology, and infusion documentation for a sample of flagged patients.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes his team will reconcile dashboard rows against appointment, pharmacy, and scheduling registers to identify administrative leakage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A chart review is a standard troubleshooting phrase that sounds concrete and low-risk; each side silently maps it onto the review method they use most often.

turns.inner_thought: The dashboard is making the pilot look clinically unsound, and I do not trust that interpretation yet. If field teams are counting temporary post-induction improvement as success and then calling relapse a treatment failure, the protocol will be blamed unfairly. I also need to find out whether pediatric high-risk colitis patients are being mishandled in surveillance planning before donors start asking whether the pathway itself is unsafe.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Ravi. The dashboard this month is showing more treatment failures and more overdue surveillance than we expected at this stage, and before the donor review we need to be clear on the real root cause rather than guessing from red flags alone.

turns.inner_thought: This still looks like classic implementation leakage to me: missed follow-ups, delayed entries, and maybe some local capacity bottlenecks getting translated into failure counts. I need to keep this bounded and practical. If we focus on recent status changes, we can probably clean the picture quickly without opening a debate about the whole care model.
turns.utterance: I agree. From an operations view, I suspect the problem is concentrated in follow-up leakage at the two sites rather than a broad pathway breakdown. I’d suggest we focus first on the cases that changed status in the last six weeks, because that’s where we’re most likely to see what tipped people into the failure and overdue buckets.

turns.inner_thought: What I need to know is whether some clinicians moved patients onto maintenance after only a brief symptomatic response, before steroid-free remission had actually held across visits. I’m especially uneasy about younger colitis cases, where a loose reading of stability can create both treatment and surveillance errors.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I particularly want to understand whether some patients were shifted to maintenance before they were truly stable, especially among the younger colitis cases.

turns.inner_thought: From the site updates, those patients were not generating urgent reviews and seemed controlled enough to remain on routine monthly follow-up, so I doubt there was reckless de-escalation. The issue is more likely that once they were considered stable operationally, the follow-up machinery became loose.
turns.utterance: That’s fair. Stability matters here, and from the site reports most of those patients did look stable enough to stay on routine monthly follow-up, which is partly why I think the leakage may be happening after that point.

turns.inner_thought: I’m still worried the protocol-defined surveillance cohort is not being captured properly across pediatric and adult services. Pediatric-onset colitis patients who have crossed the disease-duration threshold should not disappear just because they are still sitting in pediatric clinics.
turns.utterance: The other thing worrying me is that the surveillance list seems to be missing several pediatric-onset patients who should already have colorectal cancer surveillance planned.

turns.inner_thought: That doesn’t line up with what I saw on the adult registry extract. The backlog there was fairly small and mostly due to one adult endoscopy unit not assigning slots on time. If there are missing children, they must be outside the list I’m monitoring, though I assume she means the same list.
turns.utterance: I checked the surveillance list yesterday, and what I saw was only a modest backlog, mostly concentrated in one adult endoscopy unit where slot allocation has been running late.

turns.inner_thought: We need clinicians to open the records themselves: notes, pathology, colonoscopy recommendations, infusion documentation, the lot. Otherwise we will never distinguish wrong risk classification from mistimed surveillance or true nonresponse. A superficial dashboard check will not answer the clinical question.
turns.utterance: Then I think we should do a chart review this week on the flagged cases and sort out whether we’re dealing with inappropriate risk classification, missed surveillance timing, or actual nonresponse.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we can move fast on that. My team can reconcile the flagged rows against the dashboard, appointment register, and pharmacy dispatch sheets and identify where status is being overstated. That should be enough to tell us whether this is mostly reporting leakage and scheduling drift.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We can do the chart review by Friday. I’ll have my team reconcile the flagged cases against the dashboard, the appointment register, and the pharmacy dispatch sheets so we can see where the break is happening.

turns.inner_thought: If the records show that patients were de-escalated before sustained remission and proper warning-sign review, then this is not just a missed-visit problem. That would mean the pathway is being interpreted too loosely at site level, and the protocol’s credibility is at risk.
turns.utterance: And if that review shows patients were not clinically stable when they were de-escalated, then I think we have to consider that the root cause may be pathway interpretation rather than supply or attendance.

turns.inner_thought: I want to avoid escalating this into a treatment-selection debate before we’ve cleaned the operational picture. A lot of these apparent failures may vanish once overdue follow-ups are pulled back in and this month’s flags are corrected. If we can get the numbers down by next cycle, donor pressure eases immediately.
turns.utterance: Possibly, but I do think a fair amount of the apparent failure may disappear once we close the gap in overdue follow-ups and clean up the current month’s operational flags.

turns.inner_thought: I need to anchor this in clinical correctness, not dashboard cosmetics. Closing the gap means the actual high-risk patients—including those still in pediatric care—have the right surveillance and follow-up plans documented and scheduled appropriately. A prettier report without that is not a fix.
turns.utterance: Yes, but for me closing the gap has to mean that the right high-risk patients have the correct next steps documented and scheduled, not simply that we have fewer red indicators on the report.

turns.inner_thought: That’s acceptable language, and we can still execute quickly. I’ll task the site coordinators with the review using the reporting sources they already manage, and if we tighten scheduling and clean the discrepancies this week, we should be able to show improvement before the donor cycle closes.
turns.utterance: Understood. Let’s have the two site coordinators complete the chart review this week, pull together the flagged cases from both hospitals, and then we should be in a position to close the gap before the next reporting cycle.
